quote:
compress_consecutive_ranges must walk a sorted list of distinct integers and emit one [start, end] pair per maximal block of consecutive values, with an isolated value giving a pair whose two ends match and an empty list giving an empty result.

The submission handles the empty case first and then scans the list once, holding the start of the current block and the most recent value seen. The heart of it is this loop:

        for x in lst[1:]:
            if x == prev + 1:
                prev = x
            else:
                ranges.append([start, prev])
                start = x
                prev = x
        ranges.append([start, prev])

When the next value is exactly one more than the previous, the block grows; otherwise the finished block is recorded and a new one begins at the current value. The append after the loop closes whichever block is still open, so the last run is never dropped.

Finally 10 and 11 join, and the closing append adds [10, 11]. The function therefore returns [[-2, 0], [4, 4], [10, 11]], which is exactly what the specification describes. Nothing in the code compares the input against particular lists or relies on the numbers used in the visible asserts; the only test it performs is the adjacent-difference check, which is the defining property of a consecutive run. An empty list returns [] from the guard at the top, as required.
